control_implications.evidence_excerpt: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday added a critical security flaw impacting Perforce Puppet, an enterprise infrastructure-as-code (IaC) and configuration management platform, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing reports of active exploitation.
control_implications.headline: Perforce Puppet added to CISA KEV catalog
control_implications.significance: Active exploitation of a critical infrastructure-as-code platform demands immediate vulnerability management. The accountable owner should confirm affected asset inventory and remediation status.

control_implications.evidence_excerpt: On AMD-based PCs and some Intel PCs, the TPM lockout for Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs can be reset by someone who opens the PC's case, researchers at Technische Universität Berlin say. That leaves short PINs open to guessing. In lab tests, the researchers found a four-digit Hello PIN on an AMD laptop and a 6-digit BitLocker PIN on an Intel laptop this way.
control_implications.headline: TPM lockout bypassed via physical access
control_implications.significance: Physical access can defeat TPM-protected authentication. The identity and access owner should confirm authentication coverage and session revocation evidence.

paragraphs.text: Critical vulnerabilities in widely used infrastructure software are being actively exploited, with CISA adding a Perforce Puppet flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and threat actors exploiting an Apache Roller flaw for code execution. Simultaneously, a supply chain compromise of Microsoft's Agent Framework Python package on PyPI has exposed developer credentials. These developments require vulnerability and asset owners to confirm affected asset inventories and remediation status, and supplier risk owners to review dependencies and assurance evidence for compromised components.

Identity verification controls are under pressure from deepfake-enabled helpdesk impersonation and fake IT support requests that bypass authentication, while a physical attack can reset TPM lockouts to guess Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs. Additionally, the EggStreme malware toolkit has been rebuilt to evade detection against government targets. Access management and monitoring owners should verify authentication coverage, session revocation evidence, telemetry coverage, and detection test results to address these evolving threats.
